summary:
This project is an interactive video game designed to introduce young people to the real-world dilemmas of engineering. It puts the player in the shoes of an Operations Leader during a high-stakes mission to Venus.
As the mission progresses, managing the spacecraft's resources becomes increasingly critical. Supplies deplete faster over time, and as the top-screen indicators drop, unexpected emergencies become more frequent. Through this dynamic, we gamify the challenge of monitoring multiple variables at once, creating a deeply immersive experience where the player isn't just managing hardware, but protecting an entire crew.
Beyond gameplay, this project serves a deeper educational purpose: it challenges the tendency among young audiences to oversimplify space exploration. Every decision forces the player to weigh critical trade-offs—such as pushing the ship beyond its structural limits to guarantee survival, or dealing with the complications of carrying unnecessary resources.
Furthermore, the game weaves in references to real historical figures and iconic spacecraft. By doing so, it reframes space missions not just as solitary, epic adventures, but as the result of decades of collaborative effort, rigorous engineering, and shared human ingenuity. Ultimately, players walk away with a profound appreciation for the complex teamwork behind every high-risk mission.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

The project consists of a space exploration and management video game set approximately in the 2030s, in which a crew of four astronauts carries out a mission to Venus. The player must control the mission systems, manage resources, conduct scientific research, solve technical problems, and make decisions that affect the crew and the operation of the platform.

The mission is mainly inspired by the HAVOC (High Altitude Venus Operational Concept) concept studied by NASA. HAVOC proposed using a lighter-than-air aircraft to explore Venus at an altitude of approximately 50 km, where temperature and pressure conditions are much more favorable than on the surface. NASA's study proposed a conceptual crewed mission lasting around 30 days and analyzed challenges such as atmospheric entry, the deployment and inflation of the aerostat, and protection against sulfuric acid.

In our project, this idea is adapted into a fictional mission of longer duration. The floating platform is sent ahead of the astronauts, followed by the vehicle responsible for transporting the crew. The platform includes a pressurized habitat, an integrated laboratory and growing area, communication and power systems, robotics, and scientific equipment.

The habitat designed for the game measures 45 meters in length and 9 meters in diameter. This dimension is a decision made specifically for the project and is not a measurement taken from NASA's HAVOC concept.

Venus was chosen because it has extreme conditions. NASA indicates that its surface reaches approximately 467 °C and that the surface pressure is about 93 times Earth's atmospheric pressure. However, at around 50 km above the surface, NASA reports temperatures of approximately 30–70 °C and pressure similar to that at Earth's surface. This difference justifies the use of an atmospheric platform instead of building a habitat directly on the surface

What benefits does it offer?

The main benefit of the project is that it brings concepts related to space exploration and planetary science closer to the public through an interactive experience. Instead of presenting Venus simply as a science-fiction setting, the player must face problems resulting from its real characteristics.

For example, Venus's atmosphere is composed mainly of carbon dioxide and contains clouds of sulfuric acid. These conditions require the player to consider protection systems, platform stability and control, and equipment maintenance.

The project also allows players to work with concepts related to resource management, problem-solving, scientific research, and teamwork. Each astronaut has a different area of expertise, so the player must make use of the abilities of the entire crew.

The scientific aspect is also inspired by real missions. NASA's DAVINCI mission will study Venus using a spacecraft and an atmospheric probe that will measure variables such as chemical composition, temperature, pressure, and winds during its descent. Our project uses this type of research as a reference for designing the scientific activities in the video game.

What is the expected impact of the project?

The expected impact is mainly educational, scientific, and outreach-oriented. The project aims to encourage interest in space exploration and demonstrate that a mission to another planet requires much more than simply traveling there: it requires specialists, planning, support systems, research, and the ability to respond to unexpected situations.

It also aims to show that Venus is scientifically important. NASA studies Venus to understand its origin, evolution, and the reasons why it became so different from Earth. DAVINCI, for example, aims to study the atmosphere and determine whether Venus may have had wetter and more habitable conditions in the past.

Therefore, the video game aims to transform real scientific questions into situations that players can experience directly.

What tools, programming languages, hardware, or software were used to develop the project?

The project was developed using Antigravity as the main development environment and programming tool. Figma was used to design and organize the user interface. Claude was also used as development support to debug the code, identify and correct errors, and add new functionalities.

The project was mainly developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. HTML was used to structure the application, CSS to design the visual interface and layout, and JavaScript to implement the game logic, interactions, resource management, and mission systems.

The project also uses React 19.0.0 and React DOM 19.0.0. React is used to build the user interface through reusable components, while React DOM allows these components to be rendered and displayed in the web browser.

NASA's scientific and technical documentation was also used as a reference to ensure that the representation of Venus, its atmospheric conditions, and the mission concepts were based on real scientific information.

In what way is your project creative?

The creativity of the project lies in combining space exploration, science, resource management, and character-driven storytelling.

Instead of simply using a conventional spacecraft, the project takes a real NASA concept—HAVOC—and transforms it into a playable experience. The player does not simply explore Venus but must keep an aerostatic platform operating in an environment with carbon dioxide, sulfuric acid clouds, high temperatures, and changing atmospheric conditions.

The design of the four astronauts is also a creative element. Each character has a different specialization and is professionally inspired by a real astronaut:

The doctor is based on Serena Auñón-Chancellor, a physician specializing in internal and aerospace medicine who worked as a flight surgeon and later participated in Expedition 56/57 aboard the ISS. NASA records that she spent 197 days in space and participated in hundreds of experiments.

The biologist is inspired by Kate Rubins, a NASA microbiologist and astronaut. Rubins has a background in molecular biology and cancer biology and was the first person to sequence DNA in space. Her experience is particularly appropriate for our character because the laboratory and biological research play an important role in the mission.

The engineer-pilot is based on Chris Hadfield, who has a background in mechanical engineering, aviation systems, military piloting, and aircraft testing. NASA also documents his participation in Space Shuttle missions and later as commander of Expedition 35 aboard the ISS.

The robotics and communications specialist is inspired by Akihiko Hoshide, a JAXA astronaut who participated in NASA and ISS missions. Hoshide has a background in mechanical and aerospace engineering, served as commander of NEEMO 18, and later commanded Expedition 65 aboard the ISS.

The inspiration does not mean that the characters are representations of these real people. They are fictional characters whose professional profiles are based on the real experiences of these astronauts.

What factors did your team take into account?

The team mainly considered scientific accuracy, Venus's environmental conditions, technological feasibility, gameplay, and narrative.

For the environment, real data were considered, including the 467 °C surface temperature, surface pressure approximately 93 times greater than Earth's, atmospheric composition, and sulfuric acid clouds. We also considered that conditions at around 50 km altitude are much more favorable, which is one of the foundations of the HAVOC concept.

In the design of the platform, systems such as lifting gas, aerostat pressure, envelope integrity, lifting capacity, altitude, and stability were considered. These elements are related to the technical challenges analyzed in HAVOC, although the specific values used in our video game are our own design decisions. NASA's study specifically identifies the deployment, inflation, and protection of the aerostat as technical challenges.

We also considered the systems necessary to keep the astronauts alive: oxygen, CO₂, pressure, temperature, power, food, health, and crew conditions. The mission is organized around four specialists because a complex mission requires combining different areas of expertise.
